title: slot-aging-and-bank-aware-pinning-sprint-notes
content:
Sprint notes: slot-based aging + bank-aware pinning prototype

Context / motivation:
- We've been seeing recurring NVMe paging spikes and long-tail 99.9ms token latencies during mixed chat + long-context workloads. Root cause sketches in previous runs pointed to bank-level saturation and coarse LRU thrashing when the hotset moves.
- Hypothesis: a lightweight slotting mechanism that clusters related KV entries into fixed slots (time-cohorts) and a bank-aware pinning policy can increase reuse locality while reducing cross-bank hot churn and paging.

High-level design (prototype):
- Slotting: allocate a small number of rolling slots (default 32) per device. When an entry is first seen it maps to current slot id (mod slot_count). Subsequent accesses update per-entry last-slot and access counter. Slot acts as a coarse TTL/age bucket. Eviction prefers oldest-slot entries first.
- Bank-aware pinning: track per-bank hot slot scores. For banks with sustained high read bandwidth we allow 'pin budget' to reserve top-M entries from the hottest slot(s) to avoid constant spillback across bank boundaries. Pinning is ephemeral (evict-after-N-misses) to avoid long-term waste.
- Admission: new large KV pages go through a lightweight filter — if their slot is currently cold and device bandwidth > 80% they are placed into a shadow admission queue to avoid immediate eviction churn.

Experiment setup:
- Hardware: 8x A100 (PCIe gen4) per node, NVMe SLC read latency ~200us, network negligible for this test.
- Workloads: mix of conversational chat traces + long-context summarization. We replayed 3 production-sampled traces: chat-small (avg seqlen 128, bursty), chat-long (avg seqlen 1024), batch-embed (dense embeddings with stable hotset).
- Baselines: current LRU-like eviction + existing prefetch/pin heuristics (master as of 2025-08-15).
- Metrics captured: reuse_rate (per-slot + global), eviction_rate, NVMe read/s, memory_bandwidth_utilization (%), p50/p95/p99 token latency, cold-start token latency (first token after page in).

Key numbers (observed, median over 5 runs):
- Global reuse rate: baseline 43% -> slotting 62% (+19ppt).
- NVMe read/s: baseline 1280 -> slotting 840 (-34%).
- Memory bandwidth peak: baseline 86% -> slotting 69% (-17ppt).
- p99 token latency: baseline 472ms -> slotting 255ms (~1.85x improvement).
- Tail pathological case (hotset shift at t+420s): baseline spikes to 1.45s; slotting spikes to 680ms.
- End-to-end throughput (tokens/s per node): baseline 19.2k -> slotting 18.1k (~5.7% drop under sustained load).

Observations / interpretation:
- Slotting successfully groups temporally-coherent accesses; reuse_rate improvements are concentrated in chat-long traces where repeated KV footprints align to a small number of active slots.
- Bank-aware pinning reduced read fanout across NVMe channels; measured per-bank queue depth reduced by ~28% during peak windows. That correlates with lower per-request cold-read latency.
- The throughput drop (~5-6%) appears related to additional bookkeeping (slot counters and pin budget checks) and slightly more conservative admission causing fewer aggressive prefetches. But tail latency and NVMe IO reduction are more valuable for SLOs.
- Failure mode: when hotset shifts quickly (e.g., abrupt topic change), slotting shows a transient 'slot collapse' where many entries map to the same slot and eviction floods. We saw a 12s window of increased evictions — need smoothing.

Telemetry / traces to inspect:
- Perf counters: dram_utilization, bank_read_qdepth_{0..7}, nvme_reads_per_sec, cpu_cycles_slot_update.
- Flamegraph: slot-update hot path shows ~8% CPU on worker thread (worth optimizing).
- Trace link: (see linked_artifacts PR for perf dumps).

Micro-optimizations attempted during sprint:
- Reduced slot_count from 64->32 -> improved cacheline locality for slot metadata and reduced CPU overhead slightly.
- Batched slot updates: group updates every 4ms for low-priority requests reduced CPU by ~3% at cost of slightly stale slot score. No measurable effect on reuse rate.
- Pin budget adaptive backoff: simple linear decay when bank bandwidth > 85% prevented runaway pinning during long hot-stripe bursts.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How many slots is optimal for a multi-tenant mix? Need sweep: {16,32,64,128} across 10 tenant-mix samples.
- Formalize eviction priority: should we add per-slot frequency normalization (freq / slot_age) to avoid cold-but-frequently-used items surviving?
- Explore hybrid: slotting for short-lived cohorted entries + LRU for permanent model params. How to tag permanent entries cheaply?
- Evaluate end-to-end cost impact: fewer NVMe reads vs extra CPU — rough estimate says NVMe cost drop offsets CPU increase for most infra configs, but run cost model per-region.
- Address slot-collapse: ideas: randomized slot skewing (small jitter on slot assignment), slot-overlap windowing (allow two adjacent active slot ids during transitions). Need small experiments.

Action items (who/when):
- Priya: add slot_count sweep harness + automated metric aggregation (by 2025-09-26).
- Ethan: micro-optimize slot-update hot path (inline updates, prefetch metadata) and measure CPU impact (by 2025-09-23).
- Marisol: run multi-tenant replay with sudden hotset shift scenarios; capture tail delta and eviction waves (by 2025-09-29).
- Team: discuss whether to keep slotting behind feature-flag for Dedicated customers first.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- This approach sits between coarse TTLs and full frequency-based systems. The lightweight nature makes it deployable to constrained environments (edge/offline boxes).
- If we pin too many entries per bank we may artificially create imbalance; pin_budget should be proportional to observed bank_capacity and scaled down when immigration rate (new pages/sec) increases.
- Consider exposing slot-scores in console telemetry for customers to tune per-workload.

Attachments and artifacts: see linked_artifacts above for perf dumps, PR, and a small confluence sketch with diagrams.

End of notes.

Quick status: prototype promising; follow-up experiments to validate multi-tenant dynamics and hotset-shift mitigations are highest priority.
